newsitem.title: RUSSIA: NATO and Russia embrace new partnership pact.
newsitem.headline: NATO and Russia embrace new partnership pact.

text.p: NATO and Russia agreed a deal on forging a peaceful new relationship between the former Cold War enemies on Wednesday, symbolised by a warm embrace between their top negotiators.

"It is a big victory for reason, it is a big victory for the world community and it is a big victory for Russia and all governments in the world interested in peace and cooperation," a smiling Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov declared.

He clasped an arm around NATO Secretary General Javier Solana at a joint news conference in the garden of a foreign ministry mansion in Moscow after the breakthrough which ended months of negotiations described by Solana as "very tough".
The agreement, intended to placate Russia before NATO invites new members in eastern Europe, was reached on the second day of the latest talks between Primakov and Solana.
It cleared the way for President Boris Yeltsin and NATO to sign the deal in Paris on May 27, providing the text is approved by the Kremlin leader and the 16 NATO member governments.
Yeltsin told Russian Television the NATO-Russia Founding Act aimed to minimise Moscow's fears for its security once NATO expands to include former Soviet-bloc states in eastern Europe.

"We are against expansion," the president said in a rare interview. "But considering the realities, both historic and, unfortunately, in real life, it has gone too far and we have to deal with this and we minimise the risk for Russia."
A joint statement said NATO and Russia had made "decisive progress" on key issues including military problems, which had been the main obstacles to agreement.
But it gave no details of the text, leaving lingering doubts over whether they had resolved their long-standing problems or simply agreed to gloss over them.

Yeltsin's spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told Interfax news agency the president had personally played a decisive role in clinching a deal in the final days and hours. He said Moscow did well to get binding guarantees to minimise the risks.

Yeltsin himself stressed that the document followed in the tracks of the 1975 Helsinki Act -- which was approved by governments but not ratified by parliaments as Russia had orginally stressed it wanted the NATO treaty to be.
Primakov said the text of the agreement should be on President Boris Yeltsin's desk by the end of Wednesday. Solana was to forward the accord to NATO governments for approval.
"If approved, the path to signing the document in Paris will be clear," Primakov said.
Solana added: "Reason has prevailed. The road to signing on May 27 is clearly open."
The two men had worked hard to agree the final details before the target date Yeltsin had set for signing the accord.
NATO officials were anxious to conclude a deal with Russia before a Madrid summit in July at which the Western defence alliance is expected to invite several former Soviet allies to join.
Russian leaders have spoken out strongly against NATO expansion, calling it a threat to its security.
They, in turn, have been criticised by some of the former Soviet satellites who remain fearful of Moscow.
Estonian president Lennart Meri said on Wednesday Russia was still an "evil empire" for resisting NATO expansion and urged former Soviet republics and Warsaw pact states to challenge it.
As recently as Tuesday Yeltsin had said he would not sign an unsatisfactory agreement and he told Primakov to take a tough line in the sixth round of Russia-NATO talks on the pact.

A breakthrough had been blocked until now by disagreements over whether the pact should include written guarantees that NATO will not station military structures and nuclear weapons on the territory of new member states.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation has been reluctant to give such guarantees in writing.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to receive the first invitations to join NATO, although Romania and Slovenia also hope to be in the first wave.
In eastern Europe, Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati said: "Poland welcomes the agreement...which is a basis for cooperation and lowering tensions in Europe."
In Washington, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said: "We're obviously very encouraged."
But among Yeltsin's communist opponents who dominate the Russian parliament, reaction was cooler.
"(The West) has often cheated Russia and they will probably cheat us this time as well because we have nothing to trade with," Albert Makashov, a communist told reporters.
